text: A warp of thirty-two threads doesn't issue thirty-two separate memory requests when it reads global memory — the hardware tries to combine them into as few transactions as possible. Whether it can depends entirely on the pattern your threads use to access memory, and that pattern is the single biggest lever for fixing a memory-bound kernel.

If the thirty-two threads in a warp read consecutive, aligned addresses, the memory controller satisfies the whole warp with a small number of wide transactions — that's coalesced. If those same threads read scattered addresses instead, using something like index times stride, the controller issues a separate transaction per thread, and effective bandwidth can drop by an order of magnitude with the total bytes requested completely unchanged.

A coalesced warp might use roughly one wide transaction. A scattered warp can need up to thirty-two narrow ones, because the GPU fetches a whole cache line to satisfy each thread's tiny request and throws away most of it. That's why two kernels with identical arithmetic intensity can have wildly different real-world throughput.

Data layout is a common accidental cause. An array of structures packs each particle's x, y, and z together, so reading just the x field skips over the other two and spaces each thread's access twelve bytes apart instead of four. A structure of arrays keeps each field in its own contiguous array, so a kernel touching just x reads a fully coalesced pattern instead.

Watch for an index built with a multiply or an indirection — that's almost always the fingerprint of broken coalescing. Up next, lesson fourteen: occupancy and utilization, which is about how many warps an SM can actually keep busy at once.
